This sounds like it could be trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.

What to do now:
- Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
- Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
- Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
- Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.

Don't:
- Holding them tightly or covering their face.
- Offering food or water.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if she has more than one in a row, or if she might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

This sounds like it could be bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.

What to do now:
- Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
- Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.

Don't:
- Waiting to see if it passes.
- Giving food, water or home remedies.
- Trying to make them vomit.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

Still go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) promptly after washing the wound. The health workers there will look at the bite and the dog's vaccination record and decide what treatment you need.

Don't skip the visit or wait for the dog to finish its 14-day observation first. DOH offices urge immediate consultation after any bite or scratch, because rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear.

Bring the dog's vaccination card or a photo of it if you can.

"Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

It depends on the cats and the style of feeder. Some feeders let you pick how much food to dispense at each feeding. In that case, I would do half of their daily food budget in the morning and half in the evening, to match when cats are most active (and thus most hungry).

Other feeders can only deliver a fixed amount of food. In that case, you must set it to deliver that amount enough times per day to equal their daily food budget. I would still put one serving in the morning and one in the evening, and spread any extras needed in between during the day.

For completeness:
the ideal of two feedings per day is for the kitten to get a balanced diet.

It's most probably a vocalization of his excitement.

Barking is not always something negative or aggressive. Compare it to a human screaming: it can be someone screaming in rage or frustration, or it could be a child screaming in joyful play.

It could also be his way of broadcasting his presence to any potential intruder or his dog-friends in the neighborhood. His way of saying "Here I am."

Please don't give human pain medicine to your dog without your vet's advice. Many common ones, including paracetamol and ibuprofen, can cause serious harm to dogs, and paracetamol is deadly to cats.

Call your vet and describe where your dog seems sore and since when. They can examine your dog and prescribe a pain medicine that's safe for pets, at the right dose for their weight.

Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

This sounds like it could be bleeding & wounds. Most bleeding stops with firm, steady pressure. Bite wounds can look small but often get infected.

What to do now:
- If they're in pain, use a soft muzzle or towel so they don't bite. skip this if they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
- Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze for at least 5 minutes. Don't lift it to check.
- If blood soaks through, add more layers on top. Don't remove the first one.
- Once it stops, wrap it snugly but not tight. You should fit two fingers under the bandage.
- Go to the vet for anything deeper than a scrape, all bite wounds, and any bleeding that won't stop.

Don't:
- Tourniquets, unless you're trained. They can kill the limb.
- Hydrogen peroxide or alcohol in the wound. They damage tissue.
- Pulling out something stuck in the wound.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

This sounds like it could be vomiting & diarrhea. One episode in a bright, adult pet is often minor. Call your vet for advice and watch closely for the warning signs below.

What to do now:
- Call your vet and describe what you've seen. A photo helps.
- Offer small amounts of water often.
- If your vet agrees, feed small portions of bland food, like plain boiled chicken and rice for dogs.
- Keep a sick puppy away from other dogs and disinfect the area. Parvovirus spreads easily.

Don't:
- Human anti-diarrhea or stomach medicines. Some are toxic to cats and some dogs.
- Withholding food from a cat for more than a day. It can cause liver disease.

Call your vet for advice, and go in if it gets worse.

This sounds like it could be poisoning. Many everyday foods, medicines and plants are toxic. Act fast, even if your pet seems fine. Signs can take hours or days.

What to do now:
- Move your pet away from the source and remove anything left in their mouth, if it's safe to do so.
- Note what they ate, about how much, and when. Bring the packaging, label or a piece of the plant.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and tell them you're on your way.
- If it's on their skin or fur (for example a flea product), wash with mild dish soap and lukewarm water, then rinse well.

Don't:
- Making your pet vomit unless a vet tells you to. It's dangerous with some poisons and if your pet is drowsy.
- Home remedies like salt, milk, oil or hydrogen peroxide.
- Giving any human medicine.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Itching is a sign, not a disease. The three main causes are parasites (mainly fleas and mites, which are checked first), skin infections from bacteria, yeast or fungus, and allergies to things like insect bites, food, pollen, mold or dust. Itching only in certain seasons often points to a seasonal allergen.

Itching all year can point to dust mites or food.

What to check at home:
- Look through the coat for fleas or flea dirt, and at the skin for redness, scabs or hair loss
- Note where he scratches. Licking and rubbing of the feet and face is common with allergies and infections

See your vet if the itching lasts more than a few days, or if there is hair loss, scaling, a bad smell, or fluid on the skin. Please don't give human allergy pills or leftover steroids. Antihistamines often don't help dogs with itchy skin.

Anyone who is bitten by a dog is at risk of getting rabies. Consider contacting your local animal control agency or police department to report the incident. This is especially important if you don't know if the dog has been vaccinated against rabies. It is also important to report the bite if the dog appears sick or is acting strangely. If possible, contact the owner and ensure the animal has a current rabies vaccination. You will need the following information:

- Rabies vaccine license number.
- Name of the veterinarian who administered the vaccine.
- The owner's name, address, and phone number.

Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Executive Order No. 84 (1999) also calls for mass dog vaccination with free vaccines every March, Rabies Awareness Month.

Schedules differ by place, so watch for announcements from your barangay or ask your city or municipal veterinary office about the next free vaccination drive.

Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.
